history.title: History of Davao City
history.charteredDesc: President Quezon signed Commonwealth Act No. 51 on October 16, 1936, making Davao a city covering 244,000 hectares — a recognition of how much it had grown.
history.extraInfoLabel: Davao — the Melting Pot of the Philippines
history.extraInfoDesc: People from all over the country — Lumad, Visayan, Tagalog, Ilocano, Muslim, and more — have made Davao their home, shaping a city known for its welcoming, hardworking, and diverse people.

1620.title: Spain arrives in Mindanao
1620.text: Spanish forces set up control along Mindanao's northeast coast down to Bislig, but had not yet reached the Davao Gulf area.

1848.title: Spain takes control of Davao Gulf
1848.text: Spanish officer Jose Oyanguren led an expedition to Davao, defeated the local Muslim chief Datu Bago, and began the first recorded settlement in the area.

1867.title: The town moves to where it stands today
1867.text: The settlement was relocated to its current site, with Saint Peter's Church built at the corner of San Pedro and Claveria Streets as the community's center.

1868.title: The name 'Davao' is officially adopted
1868.text: The town was renamed 'Davao,' taken from what the indigenous Bagobo people called the river — Dabo, Dawaw, and Davah. Jesuit priests also arrived this year to work among the local communities.

1890s.title: A new community forms — the Kalagans
1890s.text: Some Muslim families chose to live alongside Christian settlers and were resettled in Tigatto and Maa. Their descendants are known today as the Kalagan people.

1898.title: Americans open Davao to new settlers
1898.text: American rule brought investors who cleared forests and started large farms growing abaca, coconuts, and rubber, creating jobs that drew workers from across the Philippines.

1903–1925.title: Davao grows into a major trading hub
1903–1925.text: Japanese and American plantations expanded rapidly, making Davao one of the country's top exporters of abaca, copra, and lumber, and attracting thousands of migrants from the Visayas and Luzon.

1936.title: Davao becomes an official city
1936.text: President Quezon signed Commonwealth Act No. 51 on October 16, 1936, making Davao a city covering 244,000 hectares — a recognition of how much it had grown.

1937.title: Davao City opens its doors
1937.text: The city was inaugurated on March 1, 1937, with about 68,000 residents. By 1940, that number had already grown to 98,000.

1941.title: Japanese forces occupy the city
1941.text: Davao was one of the first cities taken by Japanese forces in December 1941. They used it as a major military base, which made it a target for heavy bombing in the years that followed.

1945.title: Davao is liberated — at great cost
1945.text: The battle to free Davao lasted six months and cost more lives than any other city in the Philippines. Japanese forces continued to resist even after Japan officially surrendered.

post-1945.title: The city rebuilds and recovers
post-1945.text: With US military support and land redistribution for veterans, Davao slowly rebuilt. Farms, ports, and trade returned, with bananas, copra, and lumber leading the new economy.
